chunks: From him, from 'Abbad ibn Sulayman, from Sa'd ibn Sa'd, from Muhammad ibn al-Qasim ibn al-Fudayl, from Ahmad ibn 'Umar, who said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a man who prostrates on the sleeve of his shirt due to the discomfort of heat or cold, or on his cloak if there is a cloth or something else beneath it upon which one does not prostrate. He said, 'There is no harm with it.'
From him, from 'Abbad ibn Sulayman, from Sa'd ibn Sa'd, from Muhammad ibn al-Qasim ibn al-Fudayl ibn Yasar, who said:

A man wrote to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) asking: Does a man prostrate on a garment to protect his face from heat and cold, and from something he dislikes prostrating on? He said, 'Yes, there is no harm with it.'

key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ بِهِ: there is no harm with it

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to prostrate on one's clothing during prayer to protect from heat or cold?
ai.summary: Recorded in Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, this hadith from Imam al-Rida (AS) clarifies the fiqh of *sujood* by permitting the use of clothing as a valid prostration surface when it serves a protective function against extreme weather or disliked ground textures. This ruling underscores the Shia principle of *al-ikhlas* (purity of the surface) combined with *al-raf' al-haraj* (removal of hardship), ensuring that the physical comfort required for proper concentration (*khushu*) does not invalidate the ritual validity of the prayer.
